summary: I developed a 2D multiplayer co-op spacecraft design simulator that puts 1 to 4 players in charge of designing and operating a space mission. My game turns systems engineering into an interactive, asymmetrical co-op challenge where players take on four distinct roles: Principal Investigator (PI), Flight Systems Engineer (FSE), Ground & Operations Lead (MOS), and Mission & Launch Analyst (Trajectory). Teams must collaborate across workstations that is only accesible by themselves to balance mass, power, data downlinks, and budget before passing the Mission Concept Review (MCR) gate and launching into live orbital hazards.
details:
Players wake up in an orbital research facility's Medbay and enter the Design Lab to prepare a satellite for launch across four real-world mission profiles (Earth: Reef Lidar, Helio: Corona Polarimeter, Planetary: Lunar Ice Mapper, and Astro: Exoplanet Photometer) and four difficulty tiers (Trainee (Sandbox), Cadet, Engineer, and Director).

There are two core phases:

  1. Design Lab: Players visit specialized consoles to equip subsystems—sensors, solar arrays, batteries, antennas, and launch vehicles—while managing slot caps and hardware conflicts. Every choice triggers a "Co-Op Catch" that impacts another teammate's station (for example, high-resolution cameras generate massive science data that will overflow onboard memory unless Ground & Ops equips faster downlinks and RF licenses). Teams inspect their combined build at the Holo-Blueprint Table (Master Equipment List), tracking Concept Maturity Level (CML) and Red-Yellow-Green (RYG) margin bars before initiating launch at the Mission Control Room (MCR) Gate.
  2. Live Orbital Simulation: Once launched, the satellite enters orbit and faces dynamic environmental hazards—including eclipse battery drain, solar radiation storms, and limited ground-station pass windows—where players deploy role-specific ability cards to hit their target science score before resources run dry.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • It translates real mission-design concepts—mass/power margins, budget reserves, Technology Readiness Levels (TRL), and subsystem interdependencies—into immediate visual feedback rather than abstract equations.
  • Because no single player can see or control every detail without talking to their crew, the game naturally trains players in collaborative trade-off analysis and resource prioritization.
  • Supports solo play, 2–3 player partial crews, and full 4-player teams, lowering the barrier to entry for casual players even without any prior knowledge of spacecraft designing.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

  • Game Engine & Language: Built in GameMaker using GameMaker Language (GML).
  • Networking Architecture: Custom TCP socket networking (network_create_server / network_connect_async) with JSON-serialized state synchronization packets handling lobby configuration, role assignment, cutscene progression, real-time player movement, shared Master Equipment List updates, and synchronized launch sequences across LAN and virtual LAN setups.
  • Art & Audio: Custom 2D top-down sprites, GUI dashboards, and interactive audio cues. Some UI and sprites are found on some free use sites, and some are self drawn.

Creativity & Design Factors Considered

  • Rather than giving every player identical tasks, every subsystem was designed with cross-station dependencies so players must negotiate compromises (e.g., choosing a Sun-Synchronous Orbit for continuous solar power while accepting tighter ground-station link windows).
  • To prevent soft-locks when fewer than four players join, the briefing system automatically detects crew size—unlocking unstaffed consoles for 1–3 players while enforcing strict role-locking when a full 4-player crew is present.
  • To keep technical engineering concepts lighthearted and memorable, I anchored a story with an eccentric, 360-degree-spinning Lab Lead Scientist, guided station walkthroughs, and playful easter eggs like a mysteriously humming 1980s vending machine.
